analysis.investment_thesis: Gravita's 27.6% revenue CAGR and 58.4% net profit CAGR over nine years confirm genuine, sustained growth driven by the circular economy secular tailwind and EPR compliance mandates. However, the thin operating margins (~12%), absence of meaningful R&D, and commodity-like pricing power prevent this from qualifying as a Fisher-grade exceptional compounder.
key_strengths: Exceptional earnings trajectory: net profit CAGR 58.4% over 9 years, ROE 21.2% meeting Fisher's threshold
Circular economy regulatory moat: India's EPR compliance rules create structural demand and barriers to entry for licensed recyclers
Conservative balance sheet: D/E of just 0.20 with borrowings actually declining YoY (548→445 Cr) despite aggressive expansion
key_risks: Commodity price exposure: lead and aluminium scrap costs are volatile, directly compressing thin ~12% operating margins with no pricing power buffer
Lumpy and unreliable free cash flow: FCF was negative in FY2022 (-61 Cr) and FY2024 (-56 Cr) — a Fisher disqualifier for compounding quality
No visible R&D or innovation pipeline: this is a process-efficiency business, not an innovator — Fisher's most critical filter for long-term moat sustainability
red_flags: Other income surged to INR 111 Cr in FY2025 (34% of operating income) — source unclear, may be inflating reported profitability
Balance sheet nearly doubled in FY2025 (assets: 1,602→2,874 Cr) alongside INR 640 Cr financing inflow and INR 864 Cr investing outflow — suggests large acquisition whose returns are unproven
Equity base expanded from 837 to 2,260 Cr in a single year — dilution or revaluation event warrants scrutiny before assuming ROE durability
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Using my Scuttlebutt framework, Gravita occupies a genuinely advantaged position: it is a licensed recycler in a regulatory environment (EPR mandates) that actively rewards compliant operators and raises barriers for informal competitors. The lead battery recycling opportunity is secular — EV growth means more batteries, which means more end-of-life scrap, which means more feedstock for Gravita. Revenue scaling from INR 430 Cr in FY2016 to INR 3,869 Cr in FY2025 is the kind of long-run compounding I admire. Promoter ownership at 55.88% and FII interest at 15.75% suggest management is aligned and international institutions are paying attention.

However, I cannot call this an exceptional company by my standards. Operating margins of 11.96% are structurally constrained by commodity input costs — management has limited ability to raise prices since lead metal is priced globally. More troubling is the FY2025 balance sheet explosion: total assets nearly doubled, a large equity raise occurred, and investing outflows hit INR 864 Cr — dwarfing prior years. If this is an acquisition, the quality and return profile is unknown. The near-complete absence of R&D spending is the deepest concern: Gravita's future depends on process efficiency and regulatory access, not on any proprietary technology or product that competitors cannot replicate. At P/E 31.7x with forward P/E at 23.2x, the market is pricing in continued strong growth — achievable, but not the kind of inevitability I'd pay up for.
